title: St Patrick (17 March)
hookLine: the breastplate prayer: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me

lines: A SHORT ACCOUNT BY THE MAN HIMSELF.
cards: Green rivers, marching bands, a parade down the main street of cities nowhere near Ireland. That's one St Patrick's day. There's a quieter one, and it starts with a short piece of writing by the man himself.
In it he doesn't sound like a hero. He sounds embarrassed. He says he was not a learned man, that he writes clumsily, that as a young man he didn't really know God.
Then he tells how he was stolen from home, carried across the sea and made a slave in a strange country. The parade remembers a national saint. His own words remember a kidnapped boy.

teach.h: STOLEN, AND A SLAVE IN IRELAND.
teach.b: Patrick's own account is called his Confession. He grew up in Britain, in a Christian family, but says he paid its faith little attention.
Raiders took him captive to Ireland, where he was set to watch flocks on the hillsides. And there, alone, cold and hungry, he began to pray, he says, day and night, in snow and frost and rain.
After years of this, a voice in his sleep told him a ship was ready.
He ran, found the ship, and got home. That should be the end.

teach.h: THE VOICE OF THE IRISH CALLS HIM BACK.
teach.b: Instead he dreams of a man bringing letters, one headed the voice of the Irish, calling him, as he tells it, to come and walk among them again. And he goes back, to the country of his slavery, to spend his life there.
Tradition gives Patrick a hymn called the Breastplate, a prayer you put on like armor before going out. Whether he wrote it is uncertain; it isn't in his Confession.
But it sounds like someone who knows what it is to be alone in a hostile place.

In one English version: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Every direction covered; nowhere left empty.
Some readers hear in it the shepherd boy on the hillside, finding out he was never alone. The shamrock and the snakes come later, from legend. The Confession is where the man himself speaks.

how: Catholic and Anglican churches, and some others, keep St Patrick's feast with services and prayers, and the Breastplate is sung as a hymn or said as a morning prayer in some churches; in Ireland it is also a national holiday.

o: a kidnapped boy who chose to go back to Ireland
a sailor who carried the first Bible to Ireland
an Irish king who made his country Christian

games.q: Patrick in his own words — tap the pairs.
p: where he watched flocks and prayed

s: Patrick's own writings tell how he drove the snakes out of Ireland
the snakes come from later legend; his Confession tells of slavery, escape and his return.
Patrick was first brought to Ireland as a captive
his Confession says raiders took him there as a young man.
the Breastplate prayer appears in Patrick's own Confession
it isn't in the Confession; tradition attaches the prayer to him.

games.q: you're Patrick. you escaped slavery and you're home, safe. then you dream of the Irish, calling you to come back and walk among them. what do you do?
o: stay home; you've earned your safety.
go back to the country of your slavery.
games.why: he went back. by his own account, he spent his life in Ireland, the land where he had once been a slave.

practice: Notice each direction of the Breastplate in turn: what's in front of you, behind, the ground beneath, the sky or ceiling above, your right, your left.
If you pray, say the lines as you go, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me; if not, notice you're held on every side, by the floor, the air, the room, and rest in the middle of it.

wordCard.voice: St Patrick. A boy taken as a slave to Ireland who escaped, then chose to go back, and whose name is tied to a prayer that fills every direction with Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: christ beside me. Before, behind, above, below. I'll be here tomorrow.
